rationale: B wins because it keeps the story closer to the facts and makes the missing proof do real work. Its strongest line, "Sweetgreen says automation lifts margins — its bottom line still says otherwise," gives a finance reporter a clean tension without pretending the company has solved profitability. A has real chops, but "The $15 salad is now assembled by robot" and the claim that premium fast-casual was "supposed to be the tier where automation couldn't go" decorate the update with facts and market beliefs the brief did not give us.
gaps_in_A: "The $15 salad is now assembled by robot" invents a price point. Sweetgreen may sell $15 salads in the real world, but it was not in the supplied update.
"premium, customizable, ingredient-forward... was supposed to be the tier where automation couldn't go" is an unsupported market premise. Interesting, but not grounded enough to carry a kept angle.
"ongoing fights around restaurant-worker protections and minimum wage" adds a broad external news peg without a named current event or source in the facts.
"McDonald's, Chipotle's Autocado, etc." in the proof section drags in competitor context that was not supplied. It is acceptable as a reporting need, but it should be framed more cautiously.
gaps_in_B: "default, not the pilot" slightly overstates the facts. The update says most new stores and some retrofits, not full-chain default.
"a concrete, citable case of reduced staff hours tied to automated assembly" turns a worry into evidence. The facts say some worry about reduced staff hours; they do not prove reductions happened.
"its bottom line still says otherwise" is a sharp finance frame, but it risks implying the automation claim has already failed at company level without capex, rollout penetration, or timeline data.
The next step jumps to `journalist-fit-check` before choosing which proof gap can actually be filled. Real margin range and staffing data should decide the lane first.
